paras: The lynching of Winston Wade took place at Union City, Tennessee, on the night of September 5, 1882, when a mob of about one hundred men took Wade, a Black man, from custody and hanged him to the limb of a tree. Wade had been accused of outraging Mrs. Sarah J. Young, a white woman, near the town three days earlier. A Nashville dispatch carried the story across the country within a day, and several papers printed it under headlines approving the hanging.

According to the Nashville dispatch, Mrs. Sarah J. Young, described as 'a respectable woman' of 46, was outraged near Union City on Saturday, September 2, by a man named Winston Wade. The Clarksville Weekly Chronicle said Wade was 'charged with the rape of a white woman', and the Pascagoula Democrat-Star called her 'a white lady'. The Milan Exchange, published in neighboring Gibson County, reported that Wade was arrested and carried before Mrs. Young, who identified him. He was then confined in the court house, according to one version of the wire, or in the jail, according to two Tennessee weeklies.

At 11 o'clock on Tuesday night a mob of about one hundred men surrounded the building, dragged Wade out and hanged him to the limb of a tree. The Pulaski Citizen described the men as 'a party of armed men', and the Clarksville paper called them 'an infuriated mob'. None of the accounts names a member of the mob, describes any resistance by officers, or locates the tree.
No report of an inquest, arrests of mob members, or any official response appears in the coverage, which ends within ten days of the hanging.

The story reached most readers as a short Nashville dispatch dated September 6, printed that day in Yankton, Rock Island and Memphis and the next day in Washington, Knoxville, New Haven, Wheeling, Eureka and Sacramento. The wire text itself was flat, but editors added headlines such as 'SERVED JUST RIGHT' in the Rock Island Argus, 'Got His Deserts' in the Wheeling Register, 'A Fiendish Negro Hanged' in the Eureka Daily Sentinel and 'A Negro Ravisher Linched' in the Press and Daily Dakotaian. Others, including the National Republican and the Knoxville Daily Chronicle, ran it without comment among minor dispatches.

Southern weeklies wrote their own versions and endorsed the act. The Milan Exchange called Wade 'A black scoundrel' and the hanging 'A swift and rightous judgement', adding 'So let all such wretches go'. The Pascagoula Democrat-Star ended its one-sentence notice with 'Served him right.' Midwestern weekly digests reduced the case to a line, the Watertown Republican calling Wade 'a lecherous negro' and the Crawford Avalanche listing 'Winston Wade (colored) lynched at Union City, Tenn.' The repeated retelling produced many spellings of his name, among them Winster, Wilson, Martin and Winston Ward.

The Nashville dispatch of September 6 and the Clarksville and Pulaski papers put the hanging on Tuesday night, September 5, while the Milan Exchange said Wednesday night and the Pascagoula and Watertown papers said the 6th; the dispatch's 'last night' supports the earlier date. Accounts also differ on whether Wade was held in the courthouse or the jail, and one version gave the complainant as 'Miss Sarah J. Young', aged 40.

reader.title: Lynching of Winston Wade
bases: A mob of about one hundred men took a Black prisoner accused of assaulting a woman from the courthouse or jail at Union City and hanged him to a tree (A3, A8, A15).

Wade was taken from custody by a mob of about one hundred men and hanged without trial (A3, A8, A11); the papers tie the hanging to the accusation that he had outraged Mrs. Young, and several approved it as punishment (A2, A14).

The Nashville wire (A3, A8, A10) is matched by separately worded Tennessee accounts in the Milan, Clarksville and Pulaski weeklies (A14, A15, A18), which agree on the mob hanging at Union City while differing on the day and on courthouse versus jail.

framing.detail: Northern and western dailies ran the neutral wire text under approving or lurid headlines: 'SERVED JUST RIGHT', 'Got His Deserts', 'A Fiendish Negro Hanged', 'A Negro Ravisher Linched'.
The Milan exchange called Wade 'A black scoundrel' and the hanging 'A swift and rightous judgement'; the Pascagoula Democrat-Star closed 'Served him right.'
Washington, Knoxville and Sacramento papers printed the wire without comment under headings such as 'Hanged by a Mob'.
